claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr RHEA is single-phase BCC.
The baseline alloy has high density and insufficient room-temperature ductility.
Adding 0.5–1.0 at.% extra Hf will induce secondary intermetallic precipitation in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The precipitates will be Hf-rich and have L21, B2, or possibly Laves structures.
The secondary phase will form a nanoscale reticulated network at grain boundaries and within the BCC matrix.
Deviation from local intermetallic stoichiometry can promote nanoscale ordered precipitates within a BCC matrix.
Vacuum arc melting, homogenization, and rapid cooling will retain the proposed metastable intermetallic network.
The intermetallic network will impede dislocation motion and provide dispersion or second-phase strengthening.
Interphase boundaries in the reticulated network will deflect cracks and increase crack-path tortuosity.
The proposed network will prevent catastrophic brittle fracture while retaining compressive ductility.
Solid-solution hardening would strengthen the alloy uniformly, often sacrifice ductility, and would not modify the crack path.
The intervention will increase room-temperature compressive yield strength by 30–50% relative to the baseline.
The modified alloy will retain more than 5% compressive strain to failure.
Adding Hf will cause a slight increase in bulk density because Hf has a high atomic mass.
The baseline alloy's low room-temperature ductility results from the absence of crack-deflecting mechanisms and high screw-dislocation friction stress.
Excessive secondary-phase formation can produce a continuous brittle grain-boundary network and embrittle the alloy.
The identity and morphology of the precipitate depend strongly on cooling rate and exact Hf content.

A controlled comparison of baseline and Hf-modified alloys using compression testing, microscopy, diffraction, and density measurements can distinguish solid-solution hardening from secondary-phase-network strengthening.
